source.title: Emergent Structure in the Marginal Attention Space of Language Models
source.authors: Valentino Maiorca; Walter Nelson; Francesco Locatello

record.file_problem: Full paper text is present; no apparent truncation or garbling.
record.tranche_reason: The paper discusses representation convergence as context, but its experiments measure marginal-attention and Jacobian profiles, not representations inducing similar distances, features, or mappings as the claim versions specify.
record.gate_note: The paper explicitly distinguishes its study of attention mechanics from representation-level convergence. Its marginal-attention correlations and Jacobian results are adjacent findings, not measurements of the claim’s representation geometry. The KV-cache eviction benchmark results concern an application of the paper’s method and do not measure the claim. Rows below record relevant adjacent findings under versions ["none"].
record.test_reason: The study measures cross-model agreement of per-token marginal-attention and Jacobian-influence profiles, not representation geometry, feature overlap or mappings. The authors say they move from representations to 'the mechanics that produce these representations'. They also state that their result 'does not imply semantic convergence'. The paper cites the Platonic Representation Hypothesis as context, and its theorem concerns Jacobian statistics rather than representations. It therefore tests no version, and its findings belong under fits_no_version.
record.authors_conclusion: The paraphrase is correct. The authors also present the per-head profile as a static KV-cache eviction budget that is competitive with per-document methods, and they note that a smaller model's per-token signal can help scoring.
record.recipe_differences: The study measures correlations of marginal-attention and Jacobian-influence profiles, rather than representation geometry or distances between model embeddings as in the claim’s motivating sources.
record.method_sensitivity: Per-token marginal-attention agreement changes with the input set: it is lower on generated than natural text, near zero when compared across different documents, and lower on a whitespace-only character axis. Deleting punctuation or punctuation and whitespace slightly raises it; uniform rather than value weighting gives similar but slightly lower agreement. Per-head agreement also depends on whether profiles are compared within a model or across different architectures.

fits_no_version.finding: Per-token marginal-attention profiles agree across 67 models on the same natural document (0.867 vs consensus, 0.761 pairwise). Agreement is near zero across different documents (0.015).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: A text-specific attention-allocation profile is shared across diverse language models.

fits_no_version.finding: Agreement is lower on generated text (0.611 vs 0.867) and on scrambled text, and depends on axis restriction and weighting.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Cross-model attention-profile agreement depends on input naturalness and profile construction choices.

fits_no_version.finding: Seed-to-seed agreement rises with Pythia size from 0.78 (14M) to about 0.94–0.95 (160M/410M). Cross-family agreement emerges during training once loss beats a bigram baseline.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Shared attention profiles emerge with training and model size.

fits_no_version.finding: Per-head profiles are stable within a model (0.992) but agree only 0.373 across architectures (permuted control about 0).

Jacobian-influence profiles also agree across models, including attention-free Mamba/RWKV models (0.42–0.47 vs 0.50 for a transformer). Within tokenizer groups, agreement falls as the logit gap grows.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Shared per-token profiles follow from similar next-token predictions rather than from the attention mechanism.

record.problems: The authors state that the census is mostly English and scores at most 2048 tokens per document. The training-emergence result covers one model, one seed, and 60 short passages, with no bootstrap interval. The authors also note that their theory covers marginal influence, while the link from marginal influence to marginal attention is empirical; empirical diagnostics do not establish the uniform theoretical bounds.
record.rows_left_out: KV-cache eviction benchmark and ablation scores (Sections 5 and Appendix F) were not extracted because they assess eviction performance, not model-alignment findings. Additional per-task benchmark plots and detailed Jacobian cancellation diagnostics in Appendices D–F likewise do not measure representation convergence.

untested.parts: No representation-alignment measure against model size or capability. Seed-ceiling and training-checkpoint trends concern attention profiles only.
No vision–language representation alignment on image–caption pairs. Vision-model-vs-backbone rows compare text attention profiles.
No shared features or subspaces across seeds. Only attention-profile agreement across Pythia seeds is measured.
No mapping, stitching or relative-representation transfer of representations.
No interpretable features or circuits compared across models. Per-head profiles are model-specific but are not feature analyses.
Data and weighting sensitivity is shown for attention-profile agreement, not for representation similarity measures.
No test of plateau or causes of representation alignment.

record.verdict_notes: Results not captured as rows: Appendix E.4 (Mamba/RWKV influence vs attention consensus), B.2 (consensus saturation at about 20 models), B.6 (scrambled text) and E.5 (word-property regression). None bears on a representation-convergence version, so none needs adding as a versioned row. The authors frame their theorem as related to the Platonic Representation Hypothesis but explicitly deny that it implies semantic convergence.

versions.untested_parts: Does not measure representation geometry or test whether representation alignment rises with model size and capability.
Does not test image-caption pairs or alignment between vision and language representations as both models improve.
Reports attention-profile similarity across pretraining seeds, but does not test whether networks learn shared features or subspaces.
Does not map, stitch, or otherwise test interchangeability of representations.
Does not identify recurring interpretable features or circuits across models.
Tests data and weighting sensitivity for marginal-attention similarity, not sensitivity of representation convergence or representation-distance alignment.
Does not test whether representation alignment plateaus or whether shared training data or objectives cause it.

rows.subject: EleutherAI/pythia-410m
rows.stage_stated: pretraining checkpoints, random initialization through final checkpoint
rows.operation_detail: Measured its unweighted per-token marginal-attention agreement with four fully trained models from other families across training checkpoints.
rows.measure: Mean Spearman agreement with the reference profiles
rows.value: final step: 0.84; agreement stays near zero while loss is above the bigram model’s 2.51 bits per character and rises after loss drops below it
rows.note: The authors describe most of the rise as early and nearly complete by step 8,000; this is one model, one seed, and 60 documents.
rows.check: The 0.84 final value uses the unweighted (ω≡1) profile on 60 passages cut at 512 tokens. It is not comparable with the 850-document census values.
